newsitem.title: USA: U.S. smelters to import more aluminum - Spector.
newsitem.headline: U.S. smelters to import more aluminum - Spector.

text.p: Demand for aluminum in the United States has picked up so sharply that domestic smelters will have to import more metal this year to meet demand for their fabricated products, industry analyst Stewart Spector said.

"Because the U.S. is a net importer of ingot, rising mill product bookings means the U.S. mills will have to ratchet up their ingot imports to fill rising order backlogs," Spector said in his latest Aluminum Industry Service newsletter.

Ingot imports last year fell almost 2 percent from 1995, but this year imports could rise by 50 percent at a time when the rest of the world's economies are showing signs of better offtake of the light metal.

"With world producer ingot inventories already at minimum working levels, the only other near term supply, until producers restart idle capacity, is LME ingot, the 'stealth' stockpile, and the 57,000 tons of U.S. Government stockpile ingot that will be sold in the second quarter," Spector said.

On Monday traders said U.S. premiums on aluminum for small, promptly delivered metal have surged to more than 6.00 cents per pound over LME cash because of tight supply, partly caused by producers buying more metal than the market anticipated.
More Russian metal was coming into the country, traders said.
Spector said Western World bookings are up so far this year, and stealth stocks - metal stored off exchange - are pretty well committed to consumers for the rest of this year.
Marginal world demand - offtake that is met by LME and off exchange stocks - is well above last year's comparable level, Spector said.

"However, some time in the second period it could decline because once above ground marginal stocks have been reduced, there won't be much excess stocks left to ship," Spector said. "That is when the industry should restart the rest of its idled capacity, and not before."
Spector reiterated his price forecast of LME ingot prices could reach $2,000 per ton before the end of the second quarter.
